info.description:
The JSON API a browser and an automation client both drive (JD-016).

Every endpoint lives under /api. Authenticate either with the session
cookie POST /api/auth/login sets, or with a bearer token created by
`jaildeck token add <name>`. The Authorization header takes precedence
over the cookie, and a bad token returns 401 rather than falling back to
one, so a token client fails cleanly even while a session is active.

Swagger 2.0 cannot describe a cookie as a security scheme, so only the
bearer token appears below. The cookie works on every endpoint the token
does.

The version here is the API's and is bumped with the changelog at
release time; it is not read from the binary.
info.title: Jail Deck API

get.description:
Redirects to /api/jails, so a client that guessed the base path lands on
something rather than a 404. It is behind authentication like everything
else here, so an unauthenticated caller gets 401 instead of the redirect.

What Jail Deck did: timestamp, operation, target, the command it ran, exit
code and whether it timed out (JD-011). Filters combine, and all of them
are applied to the whole file rather than to the page.

The log lives in /var/log and is rotated by newsyslog, so after a rotation
this sees only the current file. History appears to truncate with nothing
in the response to say so: that is the accepted cost of treating a log as
a log.

400.description: A filter that cannot be parsed

post.description:
Sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict session cookie. Secure means a
browser discards it over plain HTTP on a non-loopback origin, so reach a
remote host through an SSH forward rather than binding it to 0.0.0.0 (JD-002).

Clears the cookie and forgets the session server-side. Harmless without
one, so a client that has already lost its cookie can still call it.

get.description:
Says whether this request arrived as a session or a token, and when a
session expires. Sessions live in memory, so restarting the service signs
every browser out; tokens are stored and survive.

401.description: Neither a session nor a token

get.description:
Whether <pool>/jails and its media, templates and containers children
exist and where they are mounted (JD-006, JD-021). Read-only.

put.description:
Idempotent: creates only what is absent and reports what it made. It
refuses when a dataset on another pool is already mounted where a missing
one would go, because creating it would mount over that pool and over any
jails inside it (JD-021).

get.description:
Every check this host must pass before it can run jails, each pass, fail
or unknown with what was observed and the remedy. Nothing here writes: a
check that cannot observe reports unknown rather than failing the request.

Running jails from jls merged with configured ones from jail.conf and
jail.conf.d, so a stopped jail is listed too — seeing it is how you start
it (JD-004).

Each jail carries its ZFS storage: datasets mounted at its path or under
it, and the user properties of its own dataset. Sizes are bytes, not the
1.41G zfs prints, so they can be compared and totalled.

Each dataset also carries the native properties it sets **locally**, out of
the four an existing dataset may be given (JD-023) — as the strings zfs
prints, so `refquota` reads `2G` rather than a byte count, and a client can
send the same value back. One a dataset merely *inherits* is absent: that
value is the parent's, and writing it here would create a local override
instead of changing what is in effect.

Both keys are absent for a jail with no dataset — and also when the pool
could not be read, which is logged at WARN rather than failing the
request, so an unreadable pool never costs you the list (JD-022).

post.description:
Clones a ready template's snapshot into the jail's own dataset, writes
its stanza to /etc/jail.conf.d/<name>.conf, optionally adds it to
rc.conf's jail_list, and starts it (JD-007, JD-030).

**The start is confirmed, not assumed.** `service jail start` exits 0
whether or not the jail came up, so the jail is read back from jls before
this reports it running.

**If a step fails, nothing is undone.** The response names the step and
says what exists — a dataset that was cloned stays cloned, a stanza that
was written stays written. Rolling back automatically is a second
destructive operation run at the moment least is known about the state.

The template is the full dataset@snapshot of a template that is ready;
GET /api/templates lists them with the snapshot each one offers. The
jail's root is cloned into <pool>/jails/containers/<name>, in the
template's own pool, because a clone cannot cross one.

Network modes: `alias` (one address on a host interface, needs ip4 and
interface), `inherit` (the host's addresses and its stack), `disable`
(no network, the default). `vnet` is decided (JD-017) and not built yet.

400.description: A malformed spec: see the message for the field

409.description: A jail of that name already exists, or its configuration file does

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and what exists

501.description: This Jail Deck has no storage wired

get.description:
The same shape as an element of the listing, storage included. It reads
that same merged listing rather than asking for a single jail, because a
jail present only in jls or only in configuration must still be found.

delete.description:
Stops the jail, takes it out of rc.conf's `jail_list`, deletes
/etc/jail.conf.d/<name>.conf, and destroys its dataset — in that order
(JD-030).

**Child datasets go with it** (JD-007). They are listed in `taken`. A
dataset worth keeping has to stop being a child first: `POST
/api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child}/retain` moves it out.

**Snapshots, clones and holds refuse the destroy**, with each one named
and nothing touched. Each was kept on purpose, so each goes first — and
`zfs destroy -R` is never passed, which is what would make this check
decorative.

**The last word is ZFS's.** Nothing here re-checks that the jail is down
before destroying its dataset: `zfs destroy` refuses one whose jail is
running with `pool or dataset is busy`, and a check of our own would read
the state and then act on what it read, while the mount is held the whole
time. Only one of those can lose a race.

A jail with no file of its own in jail.conf.d is refused: its block is in
/etc/jail.conf, which belongs to you and which Jail Deck never writes, so
destroying the dataset would leave the jail declared and pointing nowhere.

**If a step fails, nothing is undone.** The body names the step and says
what was already done — a stopped jail stays stopped.

404.description: No such jail, or it has no dataset of its own

409.description: Snapshots, clones or holds are in the way, or the jail is configured in /etc/jail.conf

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and what was done

501.description: This Jail Deck has no storage wired

put.description:
201 when it was created, 200 when it was already there, 409 when it
exists at a different mountpoint. Idempotent, so a client that timed out
repeats the call and the answer says where it stands (JD-016).

Five native properties may be set — mountpoint, refquota, recordsize,
compression, atime — out of the sixty-odd ZFS calls editable. Anything
else is 400 naming the list: sharenfs would export the jail's data and
canmount would stop it mounting. quota is deliberately absent, because
JD-007 puts the limit on refquota.

mountpoint may be set only at creation; asking for one an existing dataset
does not have is a 409 with both values rather than a move (JD-023).

Values are not validated here. zfs answers recordsize=7K with "must be
power of 2 from 512B to 16M", and that sentence comes back — as a 400, so
a client does not retry a value that can never work.
put.summary: Create or update a child dataset

400.description: A property outside the allowlist, or a value zfs refused

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

409.description: It exists at a different mountpoint

patch.description:
The same as tagging the jail, on a dataset beneath its own.

Worth keeping separate: a jail's listing reports its own dataset's
properties, never a child's. Tag a child with otter:instance and it will
not appear on the jail — by design, or one jail with three children would
look like four instances to a client searching by tag (JD-022).

parameters.description: Property names to values; null removes
parameters.name: properties

post.description:
The same three commands in the other direction.

It need not be the jail it left, and it need not keep the name it left
with: a dataset retained from ottermq can come back as ottermq-2's data,
which is the point of keeping it. Its properties and snapshots travel with
it, because they belong to the dataset and not to where it sits.

from is the short name from GET /retained, not the full dataset path.

parameters.description: The name it will have in this jail
parameters.name: child

parameters.description: Which retained dataset to bring back
parameters.name: source

409.description: The jail already has a child of that name

post.description:
Moves it to <pool>/jails/retained/<name>. zfs destroy -r on a jail takes
its children and their snapshots with it (JD-007), so a dataset worth
keeping has to stop being a child first.

Three audited commands: zfs rename -u, zfs unmount, zfs mount. The -u is
not optional — a plain zfs rename unmounts and remounts inside the same
command, which on a running jail is the filesystem vanishing from under a
live process (JD-025).

It still unmounts: remounted=true means the filesystem moved and a running
jail just lost that path, so stop it first. Leaving the move half done is
worse — a dataset still mounted inside a jail makes the jail undestroyable.

The retained parent is created on demand and is deliberately not part of
the layout readiness check (JD-021).
post.summary: Retain a dataset past its jail

parameters.description: The name it will have under retained
parameters.name: target

put.description:
No -r, no children. Use it when the thing worth snapshotting is the data
and not the userland: a jail's root is a clone of a template and can be
made again, which is the premise of JD-007.

delete.description:
As above, on one dataset only. Same clone and hold refusals, same
full-name confirm.

post.description:
The route that matters for a jail whose state lives in a child: rolling
the data back without touching the userland.

parameters.description: Accept losing the snapshots taken after it
parameters.name: destroy_newer

patch.description:
Sets ZFS user properties on the jail's own dataset — the tags the listing
reads back (JD-004). Returns what the dataset carries afterwards, read
from ZFS rather than assumed.

PATCH, not PUT: these merge. A replacing write would strip a tag another
tool had set, and zrepl:placeholder and com.sun:auto-snapshot both live in
this namespace on real hosts.

A null value removes the property via zfs inherit, which is not the same
as setting it empty. Only user properties — the name must contain a colon
— and the value is passed through untouched (JD-011).

parameters.description: Property names to values; null removes
parameters.name: properties

400.description: A name that is not a user property

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

post.description:
The upgrade path for a jail whose state lives in a child dataset: stop,
move the children aside, park the old root, clone the new one, move the
children back, start (JD-007, JD-026).

**Nothing is destroyed.** The old root is renamed to
<pool>/jails/retained/<jail>-root-<snapshot>, so a re-clone onto a bad
template costs one call to undo rather than a restore from backup. It is a
clone, so it occupies only what the jail wrote since it was made.

The jail is stopped and started again by this call, and ends in the state
it was found in. A jail that was already stopped stays stopped.

**If a step fails, nothing is retried and nothing is undone.** The response
names the step and lists every dataset that is no longer under the jail,
with where it now sits, so it can be restored with the call you already
have. Running a recovery automatically while the first failure is still
unexplained is how a bad situation becomes an unreadable one.

The template must be the full dataset@snapshot. There is no default:
every jail on a real host is already a clone of templates/<release>@base,
so defaulting to it would be a no-op dressed as an upgrade.
post.summary: Re-clone a jail's root from a template snapshot

parameters.description: The template snapshot to clone from
parameters.name: template

400.description: Missing confirm, or a malformed snapshot name

404.description: No such jail, no such template snapshot, or the jail is not on ZFS

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and where the datasets are

post.description:
Runs service jail restart.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

get.description:
The jail's own dataset and its children's, oldest first.

Ordered by create_txg, ZFS's transaction group, not by created. A
timestamp has second granularity and two snapshots taken in the same
second tie on it — and "which is newer" is exactly what decides what a
rollback destroys. The transaction group never ties.

name is the full dataset@snapshot, which is what confirm must equal
elsewhere; short is the part after the @, which goes in a URL.

Unfiltered. On a host running zrepl this is long — one jail on the
deployment target has 39 snapshots, 35 of them hourly.

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

put.description:
201 when taken, 200 with existed=true when it was already there, so the
retry after a timeout does not raise zfs's "dataset already exists".

The jail route is recursive: zfs snapshot -r takes the jail's dataset
and every child at ONE point in time, which is what lets a root be
re-cloned while its data stays consistent with it (JD-007, JD-024).

parameters.description: Snapshot name, the part after the @
parameters.name: snapshot

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

delete.description:
Recursive, matching what the recursive create made.

409 with a dependent clone or a hold, naming them. Both are checked by
asking ZFS first — zfs get clones and zfs holds — rather than by running
the destroy and reading its complaint, so the refusal happens before
anything destructive does. Neither can be overridden here: getting past a
clone needs zfs destroy -R, which takes the clone with it (JD-024).

confirm must be the snapshot's FULL dataset@snapshot, not the word in the
path, so a script looping over jails with one snapshot name in a variable
cannot confirm every one of them by accident (JD-016).

409.description: A clone or a hold is in the way

post.description:
NEVER recursive. zfs rollback has no way to descend into children, and its
own -r means something else entirely — "destroy the snapshots newer than
this one". So this rolls back the jail's own dataset and leaves its
children where they are; a child is rolled back through its own route, as
a separate decision (JD-024).

409 when newer snapshots exist, naming every one it would destroy. Pass
destroy_newer=true to accept losing exactly those — the refusal comes
first so the second call is informed rather than a retry with more force.

Still 409, even with destroy_newer=true, when one of those newer snapshots
is held or has a clone.

parameters.description: Accept losing the snapshots taken after it
parameters.name: destroy_newer

409.description: Newer snapshots, a clone or a hold

post.description:
Runs service jail start.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

post.description:
Runs service jail stop. Anything running inside is interrupted.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

post.description:
Turns a jail you configured by hand into a template every later jail is
cloned from — the FreeBSD Handbook's "Cloning a Jail as a Template" (17.4.3),
made callable (JD-027).

This is the general way to fill a template: it captures whatever you did to
the jail, not only packages. Installing packages into a template without a
jail is `PUT /api/templates/{name}`, which is faster and narrower.

Four commands: snapshot the jail's dataset as `@base`, clone it into
`<pool>/jails/templates/<name>`, then **promote** the clone.

The promote matters more than it looks. Without it the template is a clone
*of* the jail, and that jail can never be destroyed — `zfs destroy` answers
`filesystem has dependent clones` and names the template. After it the jail
is a clone of the template instead, which is the right way round: a template
should outlive the jail it came from, and the lineage then reads
release template → this one → the jail.

**The jail must be stopped.** A snapshot of a running jail succeeds but is an
image of a system caught mid-stride; the Handbook says to stop it first, and
taking a service down is your call rather than this endpoint's.
post.summary: Clone this jail as a template

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

409.description: The jail is running, or that template exists

get.description:
Everything under <pool>/jails/retained, with the short name a restore
asks for. Without this a client that retained something has no way to find
it again, and the whole point of retaining is that the jail it belonged to
is gone (JD-025).

Empty on a host that has never retained anything, rather than an error:
the retained dataset is created on demand.

Every template under <pool>/jails/templates, with whether it is usable and
what it was derived from.

Nothing here is stored (JD-011). `ready` is whether the `@base` snapshot
exists, which is what makes a template usable (JD-007), and `parent` is read
back from `zfs get origin` rather than recorded — so a derived template
cannot disagree with where it actually came from.

A template that exists and is **not** ready is a derive that failed part
way through. It needs no cleanup to be truthful: it is simply unusable, and
says so.

The same fields as the listing, plus **what depends on it**: every jail
cloned from it and every template derived from it, and any holds on its
snapshots.

Those are computed already — `DELETE` refuses on them — but until now a
client could only learn them by attempting a destroy and reading the 409.
That makes "can I remove this?" a question you ask by trying. Here it is a
question you ask by looking.

Both lists are present and empty rather than null, so a client rendering
them does not have to check first.

put.description:
A release template plus packages, re-snapshotted — a PostgreSQL template,
say, so every postgres jail starts with it installed (#7, JD-027).

Three steps: clone the parent's `@base`, `pkg -c <root> install -y` the
packages, snapshot the result as `@base`.

`pkg -c` chroots, so nothing is started: no jail, no stanza, no networking
for a temporary jail. It is the same shape as JD-007's `freebsd-update -b`,
which already runs against an unbooted template root.

**It installs packages and nothing else.** For anything further — `sysrc`, a
configuration file, an `initdb` — configure a jail and clone it with
`POST /api/jails/{name}/template` instead (JD-027).

**201** built · **200** it was already there and ready, so a client that
timed out can repeat the call (JD-016).

**409 if it exists but is not ready.** That is what a previous failed
derive leaves behind, and finishing it silently would install packages on
top of whatever that attempt left. Destroy it or inspect it first.

### Or prepare a release from the mirror

Send `release` instead of `from` and this builds a release template rather
than deriving one: fetch that release's `base.txz` from
download.freebsd.org into `media/`, verified against the release's own
MANIFEST. An empty `release` with no `from` means the host's own, which is
also the ceiling — a jail's userland must be the same as or older than the
kernel it runs under.

**That one answers 202 and does not wait** (JD-008). It is minutes of work;
the response says what state the template is in and the client watches the
template itself. There is no job and no job id — `GET /templates/{name}`
carries a `state` read off the filesystem and a `running` step held in
memory. **200** instead when it was already ready, which is the same
idempotent answer a derive gives.

Naming both `from` and `release` is a 400: they are two ways to build a
template, and picking one for the caller would be guessing.

A package name beginning with a dash is refused: `pkg` would read it as an
option rather than a package, and `install -y -f` is not the command that
was asked for. No shell is involved either way.

If `pkg` fails, the clone stays **without** its `@base` and the listing
reports it as not ready. pkg's own message comes back, as a `400` when pkg
ran and refused — a package that does not exist is the request's fault.

202.description: Preparing a release; watch the template

400.description: A bad name, or a package pkg refused

409.description: It exists but is not ready, or the parent is not

delete.description:
Destroys the template dataset and its snapshots.

**409 while anything is cloned from it**, naming every one. A template's
snapshot is the origin of every jail made from it, so destroying it would
take them with it. ZFS would refuse too — but only after being asked, with
a message about dependent clones rather than a list of the jails running on
them. This asks first, so the refusal is an answer.

A jail that should outlive its template is not stuck: `zfs promote` on the
jail moves the dependency the other way, exactly as cloning a jail as a
template does in reverse (JD-027).

`confirm` is the template's name. Unlike a snapshot's, it is unambiguous on
its own — a template name is unique within the pool, where `nightly` names a
snapshot on every dataset that has one.

Never `zfs destroy -R`: that would take the dependent clones this refuses to
touch, which would make the check decorative.

request_id.description:
RequestID is the caller's X-Request-Id, omitted when it sent none
(JD-011: nothing is stored that the request did not supply).

observed.description:
Observed is what the host actually said, empty when nothing could be
observed.

remedy.description:
Remedy is set on every failed check and only there: a command for a
root shell where one exists, otherwise the file or setting to change.

mountpoint_taken_by.description:
MountpointTakenBy is set on a missing dataset when another dataset, on
any pool, already has its expected mountpoint. Ensure refuses then.

config.description: Config is the file the stanza was written to.

error.description:
Error is why it stopped. The body of a failed create carries both: what
exists is the recovery information, and this is the reason it is
needed. Filled in by the handler, which is where the response is
decided -- the service returns a Go error like every other method here.

failed_at.description: FailedAt names the step that stopped, and is absent on success.

from.description: From is the template snapshot the root was cloned from.

root.description:
Root is the jail's own dataset and Mountpoint is where it is mounted,
which is the jail's path.

properties.description:
Properties are the native ZFS properties this dataset sets locally, out
of the four an existing one may be given (JD-023). Absent rather than
empty when it sets none, and a property it merely inherits is not here:
that value belongs to the parent, and setting it here would create a
local override rather than change what is in effect.

The jail's *user* properties stay at the jail level, where JD-004 put
them -- a client tags the jail, not each of its datasets.

used.description:
Bytes, not the "1.41G" zfs list prints by default, so a client can
compare and total them.

conflict.description:
Conflict is set when the dataset exists somewhere other than where the
request said. Mountpoint is settable only at creation (JD-023), so this
is not a change the API will make -- and reporting both values says more
than refusing would.

remounted.description:
Remounted says whether the filesystem was actually carried to the new
mountpoint. False when the dataset was not mounted to begin with --
which is not a failure, just nothing to carry.

blocked.description:
Blocked is set when something kept on purpose is in the way. Nothing
ran: the jail is still there, still configured, still as it was.

config.description: Config is the configuration file that was deleted.

failed_at.description: FailedAt names the step that stopped, and Error says why.

root.description:
Root is the jail's own dataset, named even when the destroy was
refused -- it is the dataset an operator would go and look at.

stopped.description: Stopped says the jail was running and this stopped it.

taken.description:
Taken are the child datasets destroyed along with the root. A jail's
children go with it (JD-007), and they go silently unless listed here.

unlisted.description: Unlisted says it was taken out of rc.conf's jail_list.

datasets.description:
Datasets and Properties are filled by the listing and by GET
/api/jails/{name}, and left out everywhere else. omitempty rather than an
empty collection on purpose: a start or restart response reports what the
operation knew, and claiming "datasets: []" there would say the jail has
none when the truth is that nothing looked.

interface.description: Interface is the host interface the alias is added to.

ip4.description: IP4 is the address for NetworkAlias, with its prefix: 192.0.2.10/24.

old_root.description:
OldRoot is where the previous root is parked. A re-clone destroys
nothing (JD-026).

parked.description:
FailedAt and Parked are the recovery information: which step failed, and
where every dataset that is no longer under the jail currently sits.

running.description:
Running is the jail's state afterwards, which is the state it was found
in unless a step failed before it could be started again.

create_txg.description:
CreateTXG is ZFS's transaction group: the only exact ordering. Two
snapshots taken in the same second share a Created, so a client deciding
which is newer has to compare this instead.

name.description:
Name is "dataset@snapshot" as zfs prints it, and is what confirm= must
equal on a destroy or a rollback (JD-024).

short.description: Short is the part after the @, which is what the URL carries.

autostart.description:
Autostart adds the jail to rc.conf's jail_list, which is what makes it
come back after a reboot and nothing else (JD-030).

hostname.description:
Hostname defaults to the jail's name, which is what an operator writing
the stanza by hand almost always sets it to.

start.description:
Start says whether to start the jail once it is configured. A pointer
because absent means yes: creating a jail and leaving it down is the
unusual request, and it should be the one that has to be spelled out.

template.description:
Template is the snapshot the jail's root is cloned from, in full:
<dataset>@<snapshot>. There is no default, for the reason JD-026 gives
for a re-clone — every jail is a clone of some template, so a default
would be a choice made silently.

clones.description:
Clones are datasets made from one of this template's snapshots -- every
jail cloned from it, and every template derived from it.

mountpoint.description: Mountpoint is where pkg -c operates and where a jail's clone comes from.

name.description:
Name is the last component of the dataset, which is what a client uses:
"15.1-RELEASE", "postgres-16".

parent.description:
Parent is the template this one was derived from, empty for a release
template built from base.txz. Read from the clone's origin rather than
recorded: a derived template cannot outlive or disagree with its parent.

ready.description:
Ready is whether the @base snapshot exists. A template is usable only
then (JD-007), and a derive that failed part way through is a template
that exists and is not ready.

referenced.description:
Referenced is the whole userland; for a derived template most of it is
still shared with its parent, so Used is what the packages cost.

running.description:
Running is the step executing right now, absent when nothing is. Held in
memory and never written down: a restart kills the work, so a marker
that survived it would be claiming something false.

snapshot.description:
Snapshot is the full dataset@base once it exists, which is what a jail
is cloned from.

state.description:
State is where this template has got to, read off the filesystem except
for the -ing forms, which come from what this process is doing (JD-008).
A template that has only been fetched has no dataset and still has a
state, because the resource a client watches has to exist from the
moment the work starts.

blocked.description: Blocked is set when something is cloned from the template. Nothing ran.

step.description: Step is the stage in the operator's words, not a command line.

mountpoint.description: Mountpoint is where pkg -c operates and where a jail's clone comes from.

name.description:
Name is the last component of the dataset, which is what a client uses:
"15.1-RELEASE", "postgres-16".

parent.description:
Parent is the template this one was derived from, empty for a release
template built from base.txz. Read from the clone's origin rather than
recorded: a derived template cannot outlive or disagree with its parent.

ready.description:
Ready is whether the @base snapshot exists. A template is usable only
then (JD-007), and a derive that failed part way through is a template
that exists and is not ready.

referenced.description:
Referenced is the whole userland; for a derived template most of it is
still shared with its parent, so Used is what the packages cost.

running.description:
Running is the step executing right now, absent when nothing is. Held in
memory and never written down: a restart kills the work, so a marker
that survived it would be claiming something false.

snapshot.description:
Snapshot is the full dataset@base once it exists, which is what a jail
is cloned from.

state.description:
State is where this template has got to, read off the filesystem except
for the -ing forms, which come from what this process is doing (JD-008).
A template that has only been fetched has no dataset and still has a
state, because the resource a client watches has to exist from the
moment the work starts.

from.description: From is the template this one is derived from, by name.

packages.description:
Packages are installed with pkg -c into the clone. Empty is allowed and
means a plain copy, which is a reasonable thing to want.

release.description:
Release prepares from the FreeBSD mirror instead: fetch base.txz for
that release and build a template from it. Minutes of work, so this one
answers 202 and the client watches the template (JD-008). Empty with no
From means the host's own release, which is also the ceiling.

BearerAuth.description: Type "Bearer " followed by a token from `jaildeck token add`.
BearerAuth.name: Authorization
